nameStory: The Mountain Plover has one of the most misleading names in the bird world! Despite its name, this little shorebird actually avoids mountains entirely, preferring flat, dry grasslands and plains. Early naturalists probably named it after the western mountain regions where it was first discovered, even though the bird itself seeks out the level valleys and prairies in those areas.
description: The Mountain Plover is a medium-sized, ground-dwelling bird that looks like a compact, earth-colored shorebird. It stands about 5-9 inches tall and measures 8-10 inches from bill to tail, roughly the size of a robin but with longer legs and a shorter, thicker bill. Its plumage is sandy brown above and pale below, perfectly matching the dry grasslands it calls home. Unlike other plovers, you won't find this bird near water - it's happiest on short-grass prairies and bare ground.

idTips.label: Dry habitat preference
idTips.description: Look for this plover on dry, short grasslands and bare patches rather than near water - if you're near a pond or marsh, you're probably looking at a different plover species

idTips.label: Sandy brown coloration
idTips.description: Overall sandy brown or buff-colored above with pale whitish underparts, creating excellent camouflage against dry soil and short grass

idTips.label: Compact build
idTips.description: Stockier and more robust-looking than most plovers, with a relatively thick, straight dark bill and sturdy yellowish legs

idTips.label: Ground-hugging behavior
idTips.description: Runs quickly across open ground in short bursts, then stops suddenly to scan for food - often crouches low or freezes when threatened

idTips.label: Plain face pattern
idTips.description: Lacks the bold facial stripes or eye-rings seen on many other plovers, giving it a relatively plain, understated appearance

habitat: Mountain Plovers are extremely rare visitors to New England, preferring the short-grass prairies of the western United States. On the rare occasions they appear in our region, they might be found on large, open fields, airports, or similar expanses of short grass with patches of bare ground. Look for them in areas that have been heavily grazed or mowed, creating the sparse, dry conditions they prefer.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare vagrant during spring migration, most likely in May. Any sightings would create quite a stir among local birders.
seasonality.summer: Not expected during breeding season, as they nest far to the west. Any summer sightings would be exceptional vagrants.
seasonality.fall: Slightly more likely than other seasons for vagrant appearances, particularly in September and October during fall migration.
seasonality.winter: Very unlikely, though not impossible. Any winter records would be highly noteworthy for the birding community.

funFact: Mountain Plovers are so adapted to dry conditions that they actually get all the water they need from eating insects - they rarely if ever need to drink, making them one of the few shorebirds that can live their entire lives without ever touching water!
confusionNotes: In New England, a Mountain Plover might be confused with other small, brownish ground birds like Killdeer (but Killdeer have distinctive double breast bands and are found near water) or even young Horned Larks (but larks have different bill shapes and behavior). Remember: if it's near water, it's probably not a Mountain Plover!
contextualKnowledge: The Mountain Plover's name confusion is legendary among birders - it's become a classic example of how common names can be completely misleading. This misnamed bird has sparked countless jokes in the birding community about other poorly named species.
compareHints: Unlike Wilson's Plover, which loves sandy beaches and has a thick black bill, the Mountain Plover avoids water entirely and has a thinner, all-dark bill. It's also much plainer-looking than most of its plover relatives, lacking the bold facial patterns, breast bands, or leg colors that make other plovers so distinctive. Think of it as the 'plain Jane' of the plover family - its subtlety is actually its most distinctive feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to Wilson's Plover, the Siberian Sand-Plover is much smaller with a thinner bill and lacks the thick black breast band.
Among its sand plover relatives, Wilson's Plover is the only one regularly found in the Americas and has the thickest bill of the group.
Compared to its closest relative Wilson's Plover, the Kentish Plover is smaller and paler overall, with a thinner, more delicate bill and lighter brown back coloring.
